claim: Schistosomes infect hundreds of millions of people in the developing world.
source: Schistosomes infect hundreds of millions of people in the developing world.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiological impact of schistosomes, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Transmission of schistosomes relies on a stem cell-driven, clonal expansion of larvae inside a molluscan intermediate host.
source: Transmission of these parasites relies on a stem cell-driven, clonal expansion of larvae inside a molluscan intermediate host.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data and observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The proliferative larval cell population (germinal cells) shares molecular signatures with stem cells from diverse organisms.
source: Here, we demonstrate that this proliferative larval cell population (germinal cells) shares some molecular signatures with stem cells from diverse organisms, in particular neoblasts of planarians (free-living relatives of schistosomes).
evidence: This claim is supported by the transcriptional profiling data comparing sporocyst and neoblast-enriched genes presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are two distinct germinal cell lineages that differ in their proliferation kinetics and expression of a nanos ortholog.
source: We identify two distinct germinal cell lineages that differ in their proliferation kinetics and expression of a nanos ortholog.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments and FISH data showing differential nanos-2 expression and proliferation rates.

claim: A vasa/PL10 homolog is required for proliferation and maintenance of both germinal cell populations.
source: We show that a vasa/PL10 homolog is required for proliferation and maintenance of both populations, whereas argonaute2 and a fibroblast growth factor receptor-encoding gene are required only for nanos-negative cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing loss of both nanos-2+ and nanos-2- cells after vlg-3 knockdown.

claim: Argonaute2 is required only for nanos-negative germinal cells.
source: We show that a vasa/PL10 homolog is required for proliferation and maintenance of both populations, whereas argonaute2 and a fibroblast growth factor receptor-encoding gene are required only for nanos-negative cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing that ago2-1 knockdown results in loss of only nanos-2- cells while nanos-2+ cells remain.

claim: A fibroblast growth factor receptor-encoding gene is required only for nanos-negative germinal cells.
source: We show that a vasa/PL10 homolog is required for proliferation and maintenance of both populations, whereas argonaute2 and a fibroblast growth factor receptor-encoding gene are required only for nanos-negative cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing fgfrA knockdown has similar effects to ago2-1 knockdown.

claim: An ancient stem cell-based developmental program may have enabled the evolution of the complex life cycle of parasitic flatworms.
source: Our results suggest that an ancient stem cell-based developmental program may have enabled the evolution of the complex life cycle of parasitic flatworms.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the molecular similarities observed between schistosome germinal cells and planarian neoblasts.

claim: Schistosoma flatworms infect 230 million people worldwide.
source: Schistosoma flatworms infect 230 million people worldwide and cause ∼250,000 deaths per year (van der Werf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Werf et al., 2003.

claim: Schistosoma flatworms cause approximately 250,000 deaths per year.
source: Schistosoma flatworms infect 230 million people worldwide and cause ∼250,000 deaths per year (van der Werf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Werf et al., 2003.

claim: Schistosome trematodes are transmitted through a life cycle that alternates between asexual and sexual generations in invertebrate intermediate and vertebrate definitive hosts.
source: These trematodes are transmitted through a life cycle that alternates between asexual and sexual generations in invertebrate intermediate and vertebrate definitive hosts, respectively (Clark, 1974; Shoop, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark, 1974 and Shoop, 1988.

claim: The schistosome life cycle initiates as eggs are excreted from a mammalian host into freshwater, releasing ciliated, free-swimming larvae called miracidia.
source: The life cycle initiates as eggs are excreted from a mammalian host into freshwater, releasing ciliated, free-swimming larvae called miracidia that seek out and penetrate a snail intermediate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the schistosome life cycle.

claim: Miracidia seek out and penetrate a snail intermediate host.
source: The life cycle initiates as eggs are excreted from a mammalian host into freshwater, releasing ciliated, free-swimming larvae called miracidia that seek out and penetrate a snail intermediate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the schistosome life cycle.

claim: Entry into the snail triggers a series of morphological, physiological, and biochemical transformations.
source: Entry into the snail triggers a series of morphological, physiological, and biochemical transformations (Basch and DiConza, 1974; Kawamoto et al., 1989; Ludtmann et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2009; Parker-Manuel et al., 2011), followed by a clonal expansion of the larvae (called sporocysts at this stage) inside the snail host, ultimately producing thousands of infective cercariae (Figure 1A) (Cheng and Bier, 1972; Ward et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Clonal expansion of larvae inside the snail host ultimately produces thousands of infective cercariae.
source: Entry into the snail triggers a series of morphological, physiological, and biochemical transformations (Basch and DiConza, 1974; Kawamoto et al., 1989; Ludtmann et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2009; Parker-Manuel et al., 2011), followed by a clonal expansion of the larvae (called sporocysts at this stage) inside the snail host, ultimately producing thousands of infective cercariae (Figure 1A) (Cheng and Bier, 1972; Ward et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the timeline of asexual amplification.

claim: Mature cercariae emerge from the snail into freshwater and burrow through the epidermis of mammalian hosts.
source: Mature cercariae then emerge from the snail into freshwater, burrow through the epidermis of mammalian hosts, migrate to species-specific niches in the host vascular system, develop to adulthood, and begin to reproduce sexually, thereby completing the life cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the schistosome life cycle.

claim: Cercariae migrate to species-specific niches in the host vascular system.
source: Mature cercariae then emerge from the snail into freshwater, burrow through the epidermis of mammalian hosts, migrate to species-specific niches in the host vascular system, develop to adulthood, and begin to reproduce sexually, thereby completing the life cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the schistosome life cycle.

claim: Asexual amplification inside of the snail is vital for propagation of schistosomes.
source: Thus, asexual amplification inside of the snail is vital for propagation of schistosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the life cycle description and the fact that thousands of cercariae are produced from a single miracidium.

claim: A population of totipotent stem cells called 'germinal cells' is thought to underlie schistosome intramolluscan amplification.
source: A population of totipotent stem cells, historically called 'germinal cells', is thought to underlie this unique intramolluscan amplification by undergoing multiple rounds of proliferation and de novo embryogenesis in the absence of fertilization (Olivier and Mao, 1949; Cort et al., 1954; Whitfield and Evans, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: Germinal cells undergo multiple rounds of proliferation and de novo embryogenesis in the absence of fertilization.
source: A population of totipotent stem cells, historically called 'germinal cells', is thought to underlie this unique intramolluscan amplification by undergoing multiple rounds of proliferation and de novo embryogenesis in the absence of fertilization (Olivier and Mao, 1949; Cort et al., 1954; Whitfield and Evans, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: Early ultrastructural and histological studies recognized germinal cells by their stem cell-like morphology and rapid cycling kinetics.
source: Early ultrastructural and histological studies recognized these cells by their stem cell-like morphology and rapid cycling kinetics (Schutte, 1974; Pan, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schutte, 1974 and Pan, 1980.

claim: Serial transplantation of sporocysts into naive snail hosts led to continuous sporocyst propagation and cercarial production.
source: In support of the totipotency of these germinal cells, serial transplantation of sporocysts into naive snail hosts led to continuous sporocyst propagation and cercarial production (Jourdane and Théron, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jourdane and Théron, 1980.

claim: Division of diploid presumptive totipotent stem cells in mother sporocysts produces progeny that can independently initiate the embryogenesis of daughter sporocysts.
source: These classic studies led to the model that division of these diploid presumptive totipotent stem cells in mother sporocysts produces progeny that are able to independently initiate the embryogenesis of daughter sporocysts (Whitfield and Evans, 1983).
evidence: This is a model based on classic studies, supported by citation to Whitfield and Evans, 1983.

claim: Daughter sporocysts can produce more daughter sporocysts or infective cercariae.
source: These daughter sporocysts, which are essentially sacs filled with germinal cells, can then produce more daughter sporocysts or infective cercariae in the same manner as they were generated themselves.
evidence: This is established knowledge about schistosome development.

claim: The process of producing multiple embryos from the same zygote with no intervening gamete production represents 'polyembryony'.
source: This process represents 'polyembryony'—during which multiple embryos are produced from the same zygote with no intervening gamete production.
evidence: This is a definition based on established biological knowledge.

claim: In planarians, a population of pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts can regenerate injured tissues and replenish a whole animal from a single cell.
source: In planarians, free-living flatworm relatives of schistosomes, a population of pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts can regenerate injured tissues and replenish a whole animal from a single cell (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002; Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002 and Wagner et al., 2011.

claim: A population of neoblast-like cells was recently identified in adult Schistosoma mansoni.
source: Guided by this knowledge, we recently identified a population of neoblast-like cells in adult Schistosoma mansoni (Collins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2013.

claim: Germinal cells in schistosome larvae have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, a large nucleolus, and cytoplasm densely packed with ribosomes.
source: Based on previous studies showing that germinal cells in schistosome larvae have a distinct morphology—high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, a large nucleolus, and cytoplasm densely packed with ribosomes (Pan, 1980)—we reasoned that nucleic acid stains that preferentially label RNA could provide a means to label these cells specifically.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pan, 1980.

claim: POPO-1 clearly distinguishes the RNA-rich germinal cells from other somatic cell types.
source: Thus, we screened a number of nucleic acid-binding dyes and determined that POPO-1 clearly distinguishes the RNA-rich germinal cells from the other somatic cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing POPO-1 staining patterns.

claim: POPO-1 strongly stains the nucleolus and cytoplasm of germinal cells.
source: In particular, POPO-1 strongly stains the nucleolus and cytoplasm of the germinal cells.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are 10-20 germinal cells in the posterior half of the body of free-swimming miracidia after hatching from the egg.
source: Consistent with previous work (Pan, 1980), we found 10–20 germinal cells in the posterior half of the body of free-swimming miracidia after hatching from the egg (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan, 1980 and imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: In vitro transformation of miracidia into sporocysts triggers germinal cell proliferation.
source: In vitro transformation of miracidia into sporocysts triggered germinal cell proliferation (Yoshino and Laursen, 1995; Ivanchenko et al., 1999; Bixler et al., 2001): we observed these cells in mitosis as early as 24 hr post-transformation (∼0.2 mitoses per animal) (Figure 1C,D), which is consistent with the behavior of these cells in vivo after miracidia penetrate a snail host (Schutte, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations and imaging data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Germinal cells are observed in mitosis as early as 24 hr post-transformation.
source: In vitro transformation of miracidia into sporocysts triggered germinal cell proliferation (Yoshino and Laursen, 1995; Ivanchenko et al., 1999; Bixler et al., 2001): we observed these cells in mitosis as early as 24 hr post-transformation (∼0.2 mitoses per animal) (Figure 1C,D), which is consistent with the behavior of these cells in vivo after miracidia penetrate a snail host (Schutte, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: POPO-1 staining identifies a similar cell type throughout various stages of schistosome asexual development.
source: Following their long-term development in vivo, POPO-1 staining identifies a similar cell type throughout various stages of schistosome asexual development, including: developing daughter sporocysts in the mother (Figure 1E); motile daughters that have broken away from the mother and migrated to the snail digestive glands (Figure 1F); and cercarial embryos developing inside the daughter sporocysts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figures 1E, 1F, and 1G.

claim: POPO-1-labeled cells ultimately segregate into a compact cluster in cercariae.
source: These POPO-1-labeled cells ultimately segregated into a compact cluster in cercariae (Cheng and Bier, 1972) (Figure 1H), presumably saved for the next stage of development after their penetration into mammalian hosts (Dorsey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Bier, 1972 and imaging data in Figure 1H.

claim: The compact cluster of cells in cercariae is presumably saved for the next stage of development after penetration into mammalian hosts.
source: These POPO-1-labeled cells ultimately segregated into a compact cluster in cercariae (Cheng and Bier, 1972) (Figure 1H), presumably saved for the next stage of development after their penetration into mammalian hosts (Dorsey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Dorsey et al., 2002.

claim: During the first 20 hr after transformation, few cells incorporated EdU.
source: During the first 20 hr after transformation, few cells incorporated EdU.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Between 20-24 hr post-transformation, 1-2 clusters of EdU+ germinal cells are typically observed.
source: However, between 20–24 hr, we typically observed 1–2 clusters of EdU+ germinal cells, which are identified by their nucleolar and cytoplasmic POPO-1 staining.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 48-64 hr post-transformation, a large fraction of germinal cells in the sporocyst incorporated EdU.
source: At later time points (48–64 hr), a large fraction of germinal cells in the sporocyst incorporated EdU, and all EdU+ cells exhibit a germinal cell-specific morphology.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All EdU+ cells exhibit a germinal cell-specific morphology.
source: At later time points (48–64 hr), a large fraction of germinal cells in the sporocyst incorporated EdU, and all EdU+ cells exhibit a germinal cell-specific morphology.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments and morphological observations.

claim: Germinal cells triple sporocyst size during the first 3 days after transformation.
source: As a result of this massive proliferative burst, these germinal cells increased dramatically in number and came to occupy most of the sporocyst body, tripling sporocyst size during the first 3 days.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data.

claim: A tightly regulated, sharp developmental transition begins at approximately 20 hr post-transformation, when the first wave of proliferation starts.
source: These results suggest that a tightly regulated, sharp developmental transition begins at ∼20 hr post-transformation, when the first wave of proliferation starts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EdU labeling data showing the timing of proliferation onset.

claim: Of the 10,852 predicted genes in the annotated S. mansoni genome, 6677 genes were detected in 48 hr sporocysts with an RPKM value above 1.
source: Of the 10,852 predicted genes in the annotated S. mansoni genome (Berriman et al., 2009; Protasio et al., 2012), 6677 genes were detected in 48 hr sporocysts with an RPKM (reads per kilobases of transcript per million mapped reads) value above 1 (Figure 2B); 1662 of these genes were upregulated relative to miracidia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 1662 genes were upregulated in 48 hr sporocysts relative to miracidia.
source: Of the 10,852 predicted genes in the annotated S. mansoni genome (Berriman et al., 2009; Protasio et al., 2012), 6677 genes were detected in 48 hr sporocysts with an RPKM (reads per kilobases of transcript per million mapped reads) value above 1 (Figure 2B); 1662 of these genes were upregulated relative to miracidia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Approximately 30% of genes upregulated in sporocysts (581 genes) share similarity with neoblast-enriched transcripts.
source: Indeed, we noticed substantial overlap between these two datasets: of the 1662 genes upregulated in sporocysts, ∼30% of them (581 genes) shared similarity (e-value < e−10) with neoblast-enriched transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of RNAseq datasets.

claim: More than 20% (864/4032) of neoblast-enriched transcripts share similarity with sporocyst-enriched mRNAs.
source: Conversely, more than ∼20% (864/4032) of neoblast-enriched transcripts shared similarity with sporocyst-enriched mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of RNAseq datasets.

claim: A total of 4749 1:1 schistosome-to-planarian orthologs were identified using reciprocal BLAST comparisons.
source: To better define the similarity between these datasets, we identified a total of 4749 1:1 schistosome-to-planarian orthologs using reciprocal BLAST comparisons (e-value < e−10) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis.

claim: 1579 orthologs were enriched in planarian neoblasts.
source: 1579 orthologs were enriched in planarian neoblasts; quite interestingly, 1525 of them (96.5%) were expressed in sporocysts as well (RPKM in sporocysts >1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of RNAseq datasets.

claim: 96.5% (1525/1579) of neoblast-enriched orthologs were expressed in sporocysts.
source: 1579 orthologs were enriched in planarian neoblasts; quite interestingly, 1525 of them (96.5%) were expressed in sporocysts as well (RPKM in sporocysts >1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of RNAseq datasets.

claim: 331 orthologs (20% of 1662 genes upregulated in sporocysts) overlap between neoblast-enriched transcripts and sporocyst-enriched genes.
source: We examined the overlap between neoblast-enriched transcripts and sporocyst-enriched genes and identified 331 orthologs (20% of 1662 genes that are upregulated in sporocysts) (Figure 2B, and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of RNAseq datasets shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The overlapping gene set may contain a core set of genes essential for stem cell proliferation and maintenance.
source: This list may contain a core set of genes that are essential for stem cell proliferation and maintenance.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed overlap between datasets.

claim: 11 out of 37 DEAD-box helicases in the S. mansoni genome are upregulated in sporocysts.
source: Strikingly, 11/37 DEAD-box helicases (DBHs) in the S. mansoni genome are upregulated in sporocysts (Supplementary file 1B), including three vasa/PL10 homologs (Skinner et al., 2012) that may play a similar role in flatworm parasites to that of vasa in other metazoans (Juliano et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2013) (for consistency with previous studies [Shibata et al., 1999; Ohashi et al., 2007; Skinner et al., 2012], we will refer to these vasa/PL10 homologs as vasa-like genes [vlg]).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: Three vasa/PL10 homologs are upregulated in sporocysts.
source: Strikingly, 11/37 DEAD-box helicases (DBHs) in the S. mansoni genome are upregulated in sporocysts (Supplementary file 1B), including three vasa/PL10 homologs (Skinner et al., 2012) that may play a similar role in flatworm parasites to that of vasa in other metazoans (Juliano et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2013) (for consistency with previous studies [Shibata et al., 1999; Ohashi et al., 2007; Skinner et al., 2012], we will refer to these vasa/PL10 homologs as vasa-like genes [vlg]).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data and citations.

claim: Vasa/PL10 homologs may play a similar role in flatworm parasites to that of vasa in other metazoans.
source: Strikingly, 11/37 DEAD-box helicases (DBHs) in the S. mansoni genome are upregulated in sporocysts (Supplementary file 1B), including three vasa/PL10 homologs (Skinner et al., 2012) that may play a similar role in flatworm parasites to that of vasa in other metazoans (Juliano et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2013) (for consistency with previous studies [Shibata et al., 1999; Ohashi et al., 2007; Skinner et al., 2012], we will refer to these vasa/PL10 homologs as vasa-like genes [vlg]).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Juliano et al., 2010 and Tsai et al., 2013.

claim: Proliferating germinal cells in sporocysts share some common features with planarian stem cells.
source: Taken together, this comparison between parasitic and free-living flatworms suggests that proliferating germinal cells in sporocysts share some common features with planarian stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The conserved germinal cell-enriched genes contain several targets accessible with available small-molecule drugs.
source: Interestingly, this set of conserved germinal cell-enriched genes also contains several targets accessible with available small-molecule drugs (e.g., cyclophilin, adenosylhomocysteinase, transketolase) (Crowther et al., 2010), suggesting that these cells could serve as a potential vulnerable point to block schistosome propagation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crowther et al., 2010.

claim: Germinal cells could serve as a potential vulnerable point to block schistosome propagation.
source: Interestingly, this set of conserved germinal cell-enriched genes also contains several targets accessible with available small-molecule drugs (e.g., cyclophilin, adenosylhomocysteinase, transketolase) (Crowther et al., 2010), suggesting that these cells could serve as a potential vulnerable point to block schistosome propagation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of druggable targets.

claim: ago2-1 transcripts are enriched in germinal cells.
source: Using this method, we confirmed that ago2-1 transcripts were enriched in germinal cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Germinal cells expressing ago2-1 also express the cell cycle-regulated gene PCNA.
source: These cells also expressed the cell cycle-regulated gene PCNA (Figure 3A top).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: More than 95% (2178/2282) of EdU+ cells expressed ago2-1.
source: Following a 24 hr EdU pulse, >95% (2178/2282) of EdU+ cells expressed ago2-1 and ∼90% (1626/1815) of the ago2-1+ cells incorporated EdU (Figure 3A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling and FISH data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 90% (1626/1815) of ago2-1+ cells incorporated EdU.
source: Following a 24 hr EdU pulse, >95% (2178/2282) of EdU+ cells expressed ago2-1 and ∼90% (1626/1815) of the ago2-1+ cells incorporated EdU (Figure 3A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling and FISH data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both ago2-1 and vlg-3 are expressed preferentially in proliferative germinal cells.
source: Similar observations were made with vlg-3 (Figure 3B), suggesting that both ago2-1 and vlg-3 are expressed preferentially in proliferative germinal cells.
evidence: This is supported by FISH and EdU labeling data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: nanos-2 is expressed only in a subset of ago2-1+/vlg-3+ cells.
source: By contrast, nanos-2 expression was detected only in a subset of ago2-1+/vlg-3+ cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: There are two distinct populations of germinal cells: nanos-2+ or nanos-2− cells.
source: This observation suggests the existence of two distinct populations of germinal cells: nanos-2+ or nanos-2− cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FISH data showing differential nanos-2 expression.

claim: The nanos-2− population expands at a higher rate (doubling time approximately 24 hr) than the nanos-2+ population.
source: Monitoring the ratio of these two cell populations over time, we found the nanos-2− population expanded at a higher rate (doubling time ∼24 hr) than the nanos-2+ population (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Following a 4-hr EdU pulse, approximately 70% of nanos-2− cells were EdU+.
source: Following a 4-hr EdU pulse, ∼70% of the nanos-2− cells were EdU+, whereas only ∼5% of the nanos-2+ cells were EdU+.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Following a 4-hr EdU pulse, only approximately 5% of nanos-2+ cells were EdU+.
source: Following a 4-hr EdU pulse, ∼70% of the nanos-2− cells were EdU+, whereas only ∼5% of the nanos-2+ cells were EdU+.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The fraction of nanos-2+ cells that were EdU+ increased to approximately 40% with an 8-hr pulse.
source: The fraction of nanos-2+ cells that were EdU+ increased to ∼40% with an 8-hr pulse, and to ∼75% with a 16-hr pulse.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The fraction of nanos-2+ cells that were EdU+ increased to approximately 75% with a 16-hr pulse.
source: The fraction of nanos-2+ cells that were EdU+ increased to ∼40% with an 8-hr pulse, and to ∼75% with a 16-hr pulse.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: With either an 8-hr or 16-hr pulse, approximately 95% of nanos-2− germinal cells were EdU+.
source: With either an 8-hr or 16-hr pulse, ∼95% of nanos-2− germinal cells were EdU+.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Following a 4-hr EdU pulse and 12-hr chase, only 6% of nanos-2+ cells were EdU+.
source: To rule out the possibility that EdU+/nanos-2+ cells are progeny of the more rapidly proliferating nanos-2− cells, we administrated a short 4-hr EdU pulse followed by a 12-hr chase period in the absence of EdU. We found that only 6% of nanos-2+ cells were EdU+.
evidence: This is supported by EdU pulse-chase experiments.

claim: It is unlikely that nanos-2− germinal cells differentiate to produce nanos-2+ cells.
source: Since a similar fraction of EdU+/nanos-2+ cells is observed immediately following a pulse (Figure 4D), it is unlikely that nanos-2− germinal cells differentiate to produce nanos-2+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EdU pulse-chase data.

claim: nanos-2+ germinal cells have a longer cell cycle and enter S-phase less often than nanos-2− germinal cells.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that nanos-2+ germinal cells have a longer cell cycle and enter S-phase less often than do nanos-2− germinal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EdU labeling data.

claim: The differential rate of proliferation likely explains why the upregulation of nanos-2 expression is delayed following transformation.
source: This differential rate of proliferation likely explains why the upregulation of nanos-2 expression is delayed following transformation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferation kinetics and gene expression data.

claim: RNAi of either ago2-1 or vlg-3 resulted in significantly fewer EdU+ germinal cells following a 24-hr EdU pulse.
source: Consistent with these genes regulating germinal cell proliferation, RNAi of either ago2-1 or vlg-3 resulted in significantly fewer EdU+ germinal cells following a 24-hr EdU pulse (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi and EdU labeling experiments shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Inhibition of either ago-2 or vlg-3 resulted in a significant reduction in the levels of cell cycle-associated transcripts.
source: Inhibition of either ago-2 or vlg-3 also resulted in a significant reduction in the levels of cell cycle-associated transcripts such as polo kinase and histone H2B, as well as germinal cell-associated genes (ago2-1, vlg-3, and fgfrA) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RNAi of vlg-3 resulted in the loss of both nanos-2+ and nanos-2− germinal cells.
source: We observed that RNAi of vlg-3 resulted in the loss of both nanos-2+ and nanos-2− germinal cells (Figure 5E), suggesting that it promotes the maintenance of the entire germinal cell population.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data after RNAi shown in Figure 5E.

claim: vlg-3 promotes the maintenance of the entire germinal cell population.
source: We observed that RNAi of vlg-3 resulted in the loss of both nanos-2+ and nanos-2− germinal cells (Figure 5E), suggesting that it promotes the maintenance of the entire germinal cell population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi phenotype.

claim: Reduction of ago2-1 levels resulted in loss of only nanos-2− germinal cells; nanos-2+ cells were still present.
source: In contrast to vlg-3, reduction of ago2-1 levels resulted in loss of only nanos-2− germinal cells; nanos-2+ cells were still present (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data after RNAi shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The absence of proliferation after ago2-1 RNAi suggests that the remaining nanos-2+ cells fail to proliferate.
source: However, the absence of proliferation after ago2-1 RNAi (Figure 5C) suggests that the remaining nanos-2+ cells fail to proliferate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EdU labeling data after RNAi.

claim: Expression of nanos-2 was reduced after vlg-3 RNAi but retained after ago2-1 RNAi.
source: These observations are consistent with qPCR quantification, in which expression of nanos-2 was reduced after vlg-3 RNAi but retained after ago2-1 RNAi (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: fgfrA is upregulated in sporocysts.
source: Indeed, fgfrA, which is essential for maintenance of adult stem cells, is also upregulated in sporocysts (Figure 6A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Table 1) and its expression depends on either ago2-1 or vlg-3, suggesting that fgfrA is present in germinal cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: fgfrA expression depends on either ago2-1 or vlg-3.

claim: Disruption of fgfrA mRNA blocked germinal cell proliferation.

claim: FGF signaling has a similar role in controlling the proliferation of stem cells in both larval and adult schistosomes.

evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular characterization and comparison with adult stem cells.

source: In light of these observations, it is plausible to suggest that neoblast-driven developmental programs inherited from their free-living ancestors may have enabled the evolution of complex trematode life cycles.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: Pluripotent cells may help worms adapt successfully to obligate parasitism by enabling both rapid expansion of an infective population and long-term tissue maintenance.
source: These pluripotent cells may help the worms adapt successfully to obligate parasitism, by enabling both rapid expansion of an infective population and long-term tissue maintenance in the hostile environments within their intermediate and definitive hosts.
evidence: This is a speculation about the adaptive significance of these cells.

claim: In Echinostoma, proliferating germinal cells are present as two morphologically distinguishable populations.
source: Our data revealing the existence of two germinal cell subpopulations (nanos-2+ and nanos-2− cells) are reminiscent of observations in some other trematode species, in particular Echinostoma. In these parasites, proliferating germinal cells are present as two morphologically distinguishable populations (Galaktionov and Dobrovolskij, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galaktionov and Dobrovolskij, 2003.

claim: In Echinostoma, one germinal cell population was speculated to be the most 'undifferentiated' cell type, whereas the other was thought to have more restricted developmental potential.

evidence: This is a speculation from previous studies on Echinostoma.

claim: Morphological heterogeneity was not observed in schistosome germinal cells.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan, 1980 and the current study's findings.

claim: The observation that germinal cells expressing nanos-2 exhibit slower cell-cycle kinetics is consistent with the conserved role of nanos in lengthening the cell cycle.
source: The observation that germinal cells expressing nanos-2 exhibit slower cell-cycle kinetics is consistent with the conserved role of nanos in lengthening the cell cycle by repressing mitotic transcripts in primordial germ cells from many animals (Juliano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Juliano et al., 2010.

claim: nanos-2 is expressed in germ cells in schistosome adult gonads.

evidence: This is supported by unpublished data from Wang and Newmark.

claim: Germinal cells in schistosome intramolluscan development are proliferative totipotent stem cells that directly undergo embryogenesis in the absence of fertilization.
source: Our results provide an initial molecular description of germinal cells in schistosome intramolluscan development. Based on the classic literature, the biology of these cells is quite unique: proliferative totipotent stem cells that directly undergo embryogenesis in the absence of fertilization.
evidence: This is based on classic literature and the current study's findings.

claim: Despite their unique developmental program, germinal cells possess a molecular signature similar to that of neoblasts in free-living flatworms and stem cells from diverse organisms.
source: We find that, in spite of this unique developmental program, these cells possess a molecular signature similar to that of neoblasts in free-living flatworms, as well as stem cells from diverse organisms.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The conserved molecular context may lead to strategies for intervening and blocking the transmission of schistosomiasis.
source: This conserved molecular context opens access to understanding these cells, and may lead to strategies for intervening and blocking the transmission of the disease.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the findings.
